title: Al-Balad: the steep path
hookLine: he has not attempted the steep path: freeing a slave, feeding in hunger (90:11–16)
tomorrow: Al-Balad: two eyes, a tongue, two lips
last: ASH-SHAMS — THE ONE WHO PURIFIES IT SUCCEEDS.

cards: Halfway up a mountain, the trail forks. One way is the switchback path, long and gentle, crowded with people in sneakers.
The other goes straight up, rocks and roots, the kind of climb where the legs start arguing before the first step. The gentle one is the easy pick, and nobody blames anyone for taking it.

Al-Balad, the city, the surah before Ash-Shams, uses this picture, a hard mountain road, and then asks a question that sounds like a riddle: do you know what the steep path is? The answer isn't a mountain at all.

teach.b: Surah ninety opens with an oath by this city, al-balad, which commentators take to be Mecca, the Prophet's own city, where he and his followers were being made unwelcome.
Then it describes a certain kind of person, loud about the money he's spent, sure nobody sees him. Verse eleven, in Pickthall's words: But he hath not attempted the Ascent.

The Arabic is al-'aqabah, a steep mountain pass, the kind of road that makes you lean forward and use your hands. Then the riddle: what will tell you what the steep path is? The answer comes in verses thirteen to sixteen.
Freeing a neck, meaning freeing someone who is enslaved. Feeding, on a day of hunger, an orphan who is a relative, or a poor person lying in the dust. That's the mountain.
Not a spiritual feat, not a vision.
Setting someone free, and feeding someone hungry. Why is that steep? Because it costs.
The man at the start of the surah spent plenty, and bragged about it. The steep path is spending where nobody claps: on a relative you're a little tired of helping, on a stranger in the dust.
Verse seventeen adds one more step: to be among those who believe and who urge each other to patience and to compassion.
The climb isn't done alone; people on the steep path pull each other up.
In the Prophet's time, freeing an enslaved person was a real and costly act, and the Qur'an names it again in Surah nine, verse sixty, among the uses of charity, next to helping those in debt.
Some readers today also hear in this verse a call to free people from other kinds of bondage.

how: Many Muslims give food to the hungry as sadaqah, especially to poor relatives and orphans, and support charities that pay off debts or free people from bondage, reading these verses of Al-Balad as a description of the harder road.

games.why: freeing a neck, and feeding on a day of hunger an orphan relative or a poor person in the dust (90:13–16).

practice: Think about food, and who near you might be hungry, or just tired of cooking for themselves: a neighbor, a relative, a coworker who skips lunch, someone you pass on the street.
Choose one person, and one way you could feed them: a meal, a coffee, a donation to a food bank.
